title: SFINAE, enable_if and Tag Dispatch
summary: **SFINAE**, "Substitution Failure Is Not An Error": if substituting a type into a template's *declaration* produces invalid code, that overload is silently removed instead of causing an error. Code before C++20 used it, through `std::enable_if`, `void_t` and tag dispatch, to constrain templates. **Concepts** do the job better now, but you must be able to read it.
markdown:
## The rule When the compiler considers a function template for a call, it deduces the template arguments and **substitutes** them into the declaration. If that substitution produces an invalid type or expression, the template is dropped from the set of candidates. The program is not ill-formed. ```mermaid flowchart TD C["the call f(42)"] --> O1["candidate 1:
requires T::value_type"] C --> O2["candidate 2:
requires T to be integral"] O1 -->|"substitute T = int:
int::value_type is invalid"| D1["silently removed"] O2 -->|"substitute T = int: valid"| K["chosen"] ``` The rule exists so that an overload set may contain templates that are only meaningful for some types. Library authors turned it into a way of **deliberately** making a template vanish unless a condition holds. > [!warning] Only the immediate context counts > SFINAE applies to failures in the function's **declaration**: its return type, its parameter types and its template parameter list. An error inside the function **body** is a hard error. This is why a constraint has to be expressed in the signature. ## `std::enable_if` `enable_if` is a trait built to fail on purpose. ```cpp template struct enable_if {}; // no member named type template struct enable_if { using type = T; // present only when the condition is true }; ``` `std::enable_if_t` names a member that does not exist. That is a substitution failure, so the overload disappears. ```cpp #include #include template , int> = 0> T half(T x) { return x / 2; } template , int> = 0> T half(T x) { return x * T{ 0.5 }; } int main() { std::cout << half(10) << ' ' << half(3.0) << '\n'; // 5 1.5 // half("x"); error: no matching function, both overloads were removed return 0; } ``` Read `std::enable_if_t = 0` as "an unused template parameter of type `int`, defaulted to 0, which only exists when the condition is true". The same device appears in three places: | Position | Looks like | |---|---| | A defaulted template parameter | `template = 0>` | | The return type | `std::enable_if_t half(T x);` | | An extra function parameter | `T half(T x, std::enable_if_t* = nullptr);` | ### The same thing with concepts ```cpp auto half(std::integral auto x) { return x / 2; } auto half(std::floating_point auto x) { return x * 0.5; } ``` The requirement is stated, not encoded. That is why [[9.04 Concepts (C++20)]] exist. ## Detecting members Two more tools make it possible to ask whether an **expression** is valid. | Tool | Does | |---|---| | `std::declval()` | Yields a `T&&` without constructing anything. Usable only where nothing is evaluated, such as inside `decltype`. | | `std::void_t` | Is `void` if every `Ts` is a valid type; otherwise substitution fails | ```cpp template struct HasSize : std::false_type {}; template struct HasSize().size())>> : std::true_type {}; static_assert(HasSize::value); static_assert(!HasSize::value); ``` How it works, for `HasSize`: 1. The primary template gives the second argument its default, `void`, so the lookup is for `HasSize`. 2. The partial specialization is tried. If `X` has `.size()`, the `decltype` is a valid type, `void_t` is `void`, and the specialization matches `HasSize` and is preferred. 3. If not, substitution fails, the specialization is discarded, and the primary template's `false_type` remains. This is called the **detection idiom**. A trailing return type achieves a similar effect for functions: ```cpp template auto printSize(const C& container) -> decltype(container.size(), void()) { std::cout << container.size() << '\n'; } ``` The comma expression requires `container.size()` to be valid and then yields `void` as the return type. ## Tag dispatch A different technique with the same purpose: choose an implementation by overloading on an empty **tag** type. ```cpp template void advanceImpl(It& it, int n, std::random_access_iterator_tag) { it += n; // O(1) } template void advanceImpl(It& it, int n, std::input_iterator_tag) { while (n-- > 0) { ++it; // O(n) } } template void myAdvance(It& it, int n) { advanceImpl(it, n, typename std::iterator_traits::iterator_category{}); } ``` Each iterator type declares its category as a tag type. The tags form an inheritance hierarchy, so a random-access iterator's tag also converts to `input_iterator_tag`, and overload resolution picks the most specific implementation available. Nothing is removed; ordinary overloading does the selection. The modern form needs no helper functions: ```cpp template void myAdvance(It& it, int n) { if constexpr (std::random_access_iterator) { it += n; } else { while (n-- > 0) { ++it; } } } ``` ## How the techniques evolved | Standard | Tools for constraining and selecting | |---|---| | C++98 | Tag dispatch, specialization of traits | | C++11 | `enable_if`, `decltype`, `declval`, SFINAE on expressions | | C++17 | `void_t`, `if constexpr` | | C++20 | Concepts and `requires` | Write concepts in new code. Read SFINAE in everything written before 2020, including most of the libraries you will use. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Is an error in the body of a function template subject to SFINAE? - Yes, any error anywhere removes the overload + No, an error in the body is a hard error - Only in Debug builds - Only for class templates > SFINAE applies to the immediate context: the signature, return type and template arguments. The body is too late. ? What does `std::declval()` do? - It constructs a default `T` for use in `decltype` - It declares a variable of type `T` + It gives a `T&&` without building one, for `decltype` only - It checks whether `T` is declared > `decltype(std::declval().size())` asks about `size()` even when `T` has no default constructor. Calling it for real is an error. ? How does `std::enable_if_t` remove an overload? - It makes the function return `void` - It throws when the function is called - It marks the function as deleted + It names a missing member type, so substitution fails > `std::enable_if` has no `type` member, so substituting fails and overload resolution ignores that template. ? How does tag dispatch differ from SFINAE? + It removes nothing; normal overloading picks on a tag argument - It works only at run time - It uses virtual functions to choose - It is the same technique under another name > A public function forwards to `impl(args, std::true_type{})` or `impl(args, std::false_type{})`, and normal overloading picks. ```
ideas:
1. Write `HasToString<T>`, detecting a `.toString()` member with `void_t`. Then write the same with a requires-expression.
2. Overload `serialize(x)` using `enable_if` for arithmetic types and for types with `begin()` and `end()`. Then rewrite it with concepts.
3. Implement `myDistance(first, last)` with tag dispatch.

cards.q: Is an error in the body of a function template subject to SFINAE?
cards.a:
No, an error in the body is a hard error

SFINAE applies to the immediate context: the signature, return type and template arguments. The body is too late.

It gives a `T&&` without building one, for `decltype` only

`decltype(std::declval<T>().size())` asks about `size()` even when `T` has no default constructor. Calling it for real is an error.

It names a missing member type, so substitution fails

`std::enable_if<false>` has no `type` member, so substituting fails and overload resolution ignores that template.

cards.q: How does tag dispatch differ from SFINAE?
cards.a:
It removes nothing; normal overloading picks on a tag argument

A public function forwards to `impl(args, std::true_type{})` or `impl(args, std::false_type{})`, and normal overloading picks.
